questions.question: Interviewing a Rwandan exporter's warehouse manager, internal auditor Uwase hears of a colleague's medical treatment, unrelated to the audit; privacy policy limits health data to tasks needing it. What is Uwase's BEST course?

options.A: Record it, since workpapers must let a reviewer redo the work
options.B: Leave it out of the interview notes kept in the workpapers
options.C: Record it, and mark that workpaper confidential with restricted access
options.D: Report it to human resources, which handles staff health matters

questions.key_concept: Information is collected and kept as policy allows: personal health details the work does not need stay out of the workpapers, however they were heard.
questions.pre_read: Does the audit need this detail? If not, what does the privacy policy say about recording it, and who else is entitled to hear it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.1 Use of Information makes policy and law govern how auditors use what they learn, Standard 5.2 requires respect for privacy, and Principle 5 covers what is said in meetings as well as records. The policy limits health data to tasks that need it, and this audit does not. Standard 14.6 asks for documentation of what is relevant to results, so recording it, the runner-up, overreaches.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: workpapers must hold what supports the results so others could redo the work. A colleague's treatment supports nothing here, and the policy bars recording it without need.
wrong_explanations.C: Restricted access suits personal data the work needs. Here the policy bars recording the detail at all, so protecting a record that should not exist misses the rule.
wrong_explanations.D: Human resources handles staff health, but no task of theirs needs this detail and Uwase has no legal or professional duty to pass it on; Standard 5.2 bars the disclosure.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the policy bars recording the detail, so restricting access to the record does not help, and D, because passing it to human resources is an unauthorized disclosure.
Final two: B beats A because documentation covers what is relevant to the engagement's results; a detail the audit does not need stays out, as the privacy policy requires.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, complete documentation means complete for the work, not a record of everything heard; personal data the work does not need is left out when privacy rules say so.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. A method step beyond the Standards
questions.question: Internal auditor Akosua, an expert analyst at a Ghanaian insurer, wants to skip the methodology's peer check of a claims-testing script, arguing the Standards set no such check. Which reply from supervisor Kwame is BEST?

options.A: Skip it: due care is measured against the Standards, not internal manuals
options.B: Skip it: a prudent, competent auditor may rely on proven expertise
options.C: Run it: the function's methodologies bind its auditors as the Standards do
options.D: Run it on scripts that support findings: care weighs cost against benefit

questions.key_concept: Due professional care includes conformance: internal auditors must follow the function's methodologies as well as the Standards, even where a step goes beyond them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what binds an internal auditor: only the Standards, or also the function's own documented methodologies? Then ask who may change a methodology step.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 4 Exercise Due Professional Care counts conformance as part of care, and Standard 4.1 makes the function's methodologies binding on its internal auditors alongside the Standards, at every stage of the work. A methodology may ask for more than the Standards do, and the step still binds Akosua. Running the check only on scripts behind findings, the runner-up, rescopes a methodology step, which Standard 9.3 leaves to the chief audit executive.

wrong_explanations.A: Conformance with the Standards is part of due care, but Standard 4.1 also binds auditors to the function's methodologies. A manual step that goes further still applies.
wrong_explanations.B: Expertise sets how well a step is done, not whether it is done. The peer check applies to experts too, and missing one's own errors is what it guards against.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: care does weigh cost against benefit, but the methodology binds Kwame as well as Akosua; narrowing a required step is the chief audit executive's call.

tips: Eliminate: A, because Standard 4.1 binds auditors to the function's methodologies as well as the Standards, and B, because expertise does not exempt anyone from a required step.
Final two: C beats D because narrowing a required step is the methodology owner's decision; the auditor follows it as written and can propose a change to the chief audit executive.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, the function's methodologies bind its internal auditors like the Standards; a step that goes beyond the Standards is still followed, not skipped on personal judgment.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Acting with integrity. A family tie handled the way the code allows
questions.question: A Namibian utility's code lets a buyer's relatives bid once the buyer declares the tie and steps aside; the file shows buyer Petrus did both, then a sibling won. Which audit view is MOST accurate?

options.A: No breach shown; check that Petrus kept out of the award decision
options.B: A breach to report, since a buyer's relative gained from the award
options.C: A concern for the ethics office, which decides whether a breach occurred
options.D: No breach, since the tender file shows the usual steps were followed

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors report conduct that departs from the organization's ethical expectations; a tie declared and handled as the code allows is not a breach.
questions.pre_read: Compare what Petrus did with what the code asks of staff who have a family tie, then ask what still needs checking.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations has internal auditors recognize conduct that departs from the organization's expectations and report it under its policies. Here the code itself provides for declaring a tie and stepping aside, and Petrus did both, so nothing departs from it. Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism still calls for checking that the step-aside held. Sending compliant conduct to the ethics office, the runner-up, treats the code's own route as a concern.

wrong_explanations.B: A relative's win is the case the code's declaration route exists for. Petrus declared the tie and stepped aside, so the facts show the code being followed, not broken.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: concerns go through the policy's channel, but only conduct that departs from expectations is a concern. Declaring and stepping aside is the conduct the code asks for.
wrong_explanations.D: A normal tender process does not deal with a buyer's family tie. The view rests on the declaration and the step-aside, which the auditor still checks held.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the code expects such ties to be declared and set aside, not to bar the relative's firm, and D, because the usual tender steps say nothing about the buyer's family tie.
Final two: A beats C because Standard 1.2 sends conduct that departs from expectations through the ethics channel; conduct that follows the code's own route is checked, not referred.

Exam cue: on CIA questions, compare the conduct with the organization's stated expectations before reporting; a tie declared and managed as policy allows is not a breach, though the auditor verifies it.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. A stake in the result without a former role
questions.question: As a finance analyst two years ago, internal auditor Lena wrote a Swedish insurer's losing business case against outsourcing claims handling; Lena is now assigned assurance on the outsourced service. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: No impairment, since the case was written over 12 months ago
options.B: A possible impairment, for Lena to disclose to the activity's management
options.C: No impairment, since a supervisor will review Lena's workpapers
options.D: A possible impairment, for Lena to disclose to a designated supervisor

questions.key_concept: Objectivity can be impaired by a stake in an outcome, not only by past responsibility; a possible or perceived impairment is disclosed.
questions.pre_read: What would Lena gain if the outsourced service looked poor, and how might others read Lena's findings? Then ask who must hear about it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity requires internal auditors to know and manage their possible biases, and Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity counts potential and perceived impairments, not only actual ones. Poor results would vindicate Lena's losing case, and others could read them that way. Standard 2.3 requires disclosure to the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor. The 12-month rule, the runner-up, concerns past responsibility for an activity, which Lena never had.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the 12-month presumption covers assurance on an activity the auditor once ran. Lena never ran claims, and a stake in the result does not simply lapse with time.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 2.3 has an auditor tell the chief audit executive, or a supervisor that executive designates. Raising it with the activity's management is the executive's call.
wrong_explanations.C: Supervisory review checks the work, but it does not remove Lena's stake in the outcome or how others see it. An impairment that may affect objectivity must be disclosed.

tips: Eliminate: B, because in assurance work the auditor tells the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor, not the activity's management, and C, because review does not remove a stake in the outcome.
Final two: D beats A because any situation that may sway judgment can impair objectivity; the 12-month presumption covers former responsibility for an activity, which Lena never held.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, ask whether the auditor has a stake in how the results look, not only whether they once ran the activity; a possible impairment is disclosed.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. A disagreement inside the audit team
questions.question: Internal auditor Ayesha and engagement supervisor Bilal still disagree, after reviewing the evidence together, on whether a Pakistani textile mill's late boiler inspections amount to a finding. What is Ayesha's BEST next step?

options.A: Set out both views in the final communication for management
options.B: Seek further evidence, and record both views in the workpapers
options.C: Adopt Bilal's view, since the supervisor approves the engagement work
options.D: Seek further evidence, and let the mill's managers rule on the finding

questions.key_concept: A difference in professional judgment inside the audit team is settled by more inquiry and documented views, not deference to rank.
questions.pre_read: Who disagrees here, two auditors or the auditors and management? Each kind of disagreement has its own route and its own record.
questions.correct_explanation: The considerations to Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance have the chief audit executive set a way to settle judgment differences inside the team, such as more fact-finding and a workpaper record of each view. The considerations to Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity describe objectivity as never handing one's judgment over to someone else. Adopting the supervisor's view, the runner-up, skips that fact-finding and yields to rank.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard 13.1 puts both sides' positions on record when auditors and management disagree. This dispute is inside the audit team, so it is settled within the function.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: supervisors guide and review the work, but objectivity means not handing judgment to rank. Differences are resolved on further evidence, with both views documented.
wrong_explanations.D: Further evidence helps, and management can explain causes, but it does not rule on whether the audit team's finding exists; that judgment stays inside the function.

tips: Eliminate: A, because both positions go into the final communication when auditors and management disagree, not when two auditors do, and D, because management does not rule on the team's own finding.
Final two: B beats C because a difference in professional judgment is resolved by facts and further inquiry, with both views documented; deferring to rank leaves the question unexamined.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, check who disagrees: auditor against management goes to the positions in the final communication; auditor against auditor is settled inside the function on the evidence.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Technical terms for a nontechnical reader
questions.question: Internal auditor Hamid's draft finding for a Moroccan olive-oil exporter's warehouse manager turns on 'privileged accounts' and uses other IT terms throughout. Which revision is BEST?

options.A: Rewrite in everyday words, explaining the terms the finding needs
options.B: Rewrite in everyday words, leaving out terms with no everyday equivalent
options.C: Drop the access detail, since a concise draft leaves out technicalities
options.D: Keep the wording, and append a glossary of the IT terms

questions.key_concept: Clear communication uses the reader's own terms, avoids technical language the reader does not need, and defines the terms that must stay.
questions.pre_read: Who reads this draft, and which words would that reader already use? Clarity is judged by the intended reader, not the writer.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.2 Effective Communication requires methodologies for clear communication, and its considerations measure clarity from the intended reader's side: the organization's everyday vocabulary, no jargon the message can do without, and a short definition for any specialist term that has to stay. The finding turns on privileged accounts, so that term stays and is explained. Dropping every term without an everyday equivalent, the runner-up, loses what the finding is about.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: plain words help, but an important term with no everyday equivalent is defined, not dropped. Leaving it out loses what the finding is about.
wrong_explanations.C: Concise means cutting what is unnecessary, not the significant details that support a finding. Clarity improves when those details stay.
wrong_explanations.D: Defining terms helps, but clarity also means avoiding technical language the reader does not need. A glossary at the back leaves the jargon in every sentence.

tips: Eliminate: C, because concise removes unnecessary words, not the details that support the finding, and D, because a glossary at the back leaves needless jargon in every sentence.
Final two: A beats B because a term the finding depends on is kept and explained, not dropped; plain words replace only the jargon the message can do without.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, clear communication is judged from the intended reader's side: their terms, no needless jargon, defined terms where unavoidable, supporting detail kept.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. A legal duty that covers part of a request
questions.question: Counsel confirms a regulator's notice lawfully requires a Peruvian fishmeal maker's emission-testing workpapers; the inspector also wants overtime workpapers, which no law or policy authorizes releasing. What is chief audit executive Rosa's BEST response?

options.A: Release both sets, since the inspector holds lawful authority
options.B: Release neither until the board approves an outside release
options.C: Release the emission workpapers, and decline the overtime request
options.D: Release both sets, with staff names removed from the overtime set

questions.key_concept: A legal duty permits disclosing confidential information only as far as the duty reaches; anything beyond it stays with authorized parties.
questions.pre_read: Note what counsel confirmed and what the stem says about any authority to release the workpapers.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.2 Protection of Information bars giving confidential information to unauthorized parties unless a legal or professional responsibility requires it, and Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior requires the disclosures the law demands. Counsel confirms the notice reaches the emission workpapers, so those go. No law or policy authorizes releasing the overtime workpapers, so the inspector is an unauthorized party for them. Removing names, the runner-up, still discloses work no duty or authorization covers.

wrong_explanations.A: Authority to demand some records is not authority to receive all. The notice covers the emission workpapers; nothing requires or authorizes releasing the overtime set.
wrong_explanations.B: A lawful notice is a legal duty to disclose, and Standard 1.3 requires meeting it. Internal approval routes cannot hold back what the law requires.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: removing names suits a disclosure that is owed but must protect privacy. No duty or authorization covers the overtime workpapers, and redaction does not supply one.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the notice sets how far the legal duty reaches, and B, because the owed release cannot hinge on the board's approval; internal review may come first but cannot block it.

Final two: C beats D because confidential information goes outside only to an authorized party or under a legal duty; redaction protects people in an owed disclosure but does not authorize an unowed one.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a legal duty to disclose opens the door only as wide as the duty; anything beyond it needs its own authorization, or it stays confidential.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. Judging one's own earlier audit conclusion
questions.question: Internal auditor Ana rated a Vietnamese hotel group's payroll controls effective last year; a fraud spanning that year has surfaced, and Ana is assigned to assess how it evaded them. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Objectivity intact: running payroll was not Ana's responsibility
options.B: Objectivity intact: Ana's knowledge of those controls speeds the review
options.C: Objectivity at risk: the fraud suggests Ana's earlier work lacked care
options.D: Objectivity at risk: the review would judge the rating that Ana gave

questions.key_concept: The risk of self-review bias arises whenever auditors would judge their own earlier work, an audit conclusion included, not only an activity they once ran.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the engagement would have to evaluate, then test each option's reason against the facts, not only its conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity names self-review bias, the weaker critical eye people bring to their own work, and Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity counts impairments in appearance as well as in fact. Explaining how the fraud passed controls Ana rated effective means judging Ana's own rating, so objectivity is impaired at least in appearance and Ana discloses it under Standard 2.3. Never having run payroll, the runner-up, settles only the former-responsibility rule.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the refrain rule and the 12-month presumption concern running an activity, but self-review bias also covers judging one's own past audit work, as here.
wrong_explanations.B: Familiarity with one's own earlier view makes a fresh look harder, not easier. Knowing an area best is the warning sign when that earlier view is under review.
wrong_explanations.C: Due care is not infallibility, and controls give only reasonable assurance, so a later fraud alone does not mean poor work. The risk is Ana's stake in the rating.

tips: Eliminate: B, because familiarity with one's own earlier view weakens a critical review rather than helping it, and C, because a fraud found later does not prove the earlier work lacked due care.
Final two: D beats A because self-review bias covers judging one's own past work, an audit rating included; the refrain rule on former responsibility does not set its limit.

Exam cue: on CIA questions, ask whose work the engagement would judge; if it is the assigned auditor's own conclusion, objectivity is impaired at least in appearance, though they never ran the activity.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. A good practice other units could use
questions.question: Auditing a Finnish dairy's three depots, internal auditor Aino finds one depot's route planning cuts fuel use by a fifth; the draft lists only the four findings. Which advice from the engagement supervisor is BEST?

options.A: Leave it out, since a concise draft is limited to the findings
options.B: Add it, noting that the other depots could adopt the practice
options.C: Leave it for the chief audit executive's themes report to the board
options.D: Mention it to that depot's manager at the closing meeting

questions.key_concept: Engagement communications should acknowledge good performance too; a practice others could adopt is worth reporting, not only the gaps.
questions.pre_read: Is the depot's practice inside the engagement, and who else could use it? Then ask what a complete, constructive communication contains.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.3 Communicating Results' considerations ask the chief audit executive to encourage auditors to acknowledge satisfactory performance, noting that good practices may carry over to other parts of the organization. Standard 11.2 Effective Communication asks for constructive communications that help improvement. The practice sits inside the engagement and could serve the other depots. A word at the closing meeting, the runner-up, reaches one manager and leaves the other depots unaware.

wrong_explanations.A: Concise means leaving out what is unnecessary or unrelated. A practice inside the engagement that could cut fuel use at other depots is neither.
wrong_explanations.C: Themes come from patterns across several engagements and go to the board and senior management. A practice found in this engagement is acknowledged in its own communication.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: telling the manager builds the relationship, but the benefit lies in the other depots adopting the practice, which needs it in the communication.

tips: Eliminate: A, because concise cuts unnecessary or unrelated detail, not a relevant practice, and C, because themes draw on several engagements; a practice found here is acknowledged in this engagement's communication.
Final two: B beats D because a practice other units could adopt belongs in the engagement communication; a remark to one manager keeps the benefit at one depot.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, engagement communications should acknowledge good practice the evidence shows, especially one other units could adopt, not only the findings.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. Access left over from a closed engagement
questions.question: Internal auditor Andre still holds the HR system access granted for a Belizean bank's payroll engagement, now closed; follow-up will use evidence management sends. Which view of that access is MOST accurate?

options.A: It should go now: access ends when the work needing it ends
options.B: It should stay: the charter grants internal audit unrestricted access
options.C: It should go at the chief audit executive's next periodic access review
options.D: It should stay until follow-up closes, then be removed

questions.key_concept: Access to information is granted for the work; once the work no longer needs it, the access should be removed and requested again later.
questions.pre_read: List the work still ahead and what each step will rely on before judging the access.
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality keeps information for professional purposes, and Standard 5.2 Protection of Information requires managing the risk of accidental exposure, naming access and copies no longer needed among the function's concerns. Its considerations add that permissions should be revoked once the work no longer needs them. Keeping it until follow-up closes, the runner-up, overlooks that follow-up uses management's evidence, so no remaining work needs the access.

wrong_explanations.B: Unrestricted access lets internal auditors reach what their work needs. It does not mean standing access to personal data after the work is done.
wrong_explanations.C: The chief audit executive's periodic review of access needs is a backstop. Andre already knows the need has ended, and holding the access until then only adds exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: access may stay while work still needs it, but this follow-up uses evidence management sends. Nothing needs the access now, so holding it only adds exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B, because unrestricted access covers what the work needs, not standing access afterward, and C, because the periodic access review is a backstop, not a reason to hold access no work needs.
Final two: A beats D because the follow-up relies on management's evidence, so no remaining work needs the access; it should be removed now and requested again if needed.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, access follows the work: granted when needed, removed when the need ends, and requested again for the next engagement.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Objectivity impairments of individual auditors. A short acting role in the activity
questions.question: Five months ago internal auditor Chikondi spent three weeks as a Malawian tea estate's acting dispatch manager, on an approved rotation. Which view of Chikondi giving assurance on dispatch's past year is MOST accurate?

options.A: Not presumed impaired: three weeks of cover is too brief to count
options.B: Not presumed impaired: the chief audit executive approved the rotation
options.C: Presumed impaired for the weeks Chikondi was in charge, not the rest
options.D: Presumed impaired: covering as manager counts as holding responsibility

questions.key_concept: Any responsibility for an activity within the previous 12 months, however brief or approved, makes objectivity presumed impaired for assurance on that activity.
questions.pre_read: Did Chikondi hold responsibility for dispatch, and when? Then ask whether the length of the role or its approval changes the rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity bars assessing an activity one was responsible for and presumes impairment for assurance when that responsibility fell within the previous 12 months. Acting as dispatch manager was responsibility for dispatch, five months ago. The rule sets no minimum length, so a short spell, the runner-up's ground, still counts, and the presumption covers the activity under review, not only the weeks Chikondi ran it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the Standards set no minimum period. Three weeks in charge of dispatch is responsibility for it, and five months ago is inside the 12 months.
wrong_explanations.B: Approving a rotation decides who covers the role, not whether objectivity is impaired. Standard 2.2's presumption follows the responsibility held, whoever approved it.
wrong_explanations.C: The presumption attaches to the activity Chikondi was responsible for. Testing only the other weeks would still have Chikondi judging a process, staff and decisions Chikondi ran.

tips: Eliminate: B, because approving a rotation does not cure the impairment it creates, and C, because the presumption covers the activity under review, not only the weeks Chikondi was in charge.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 2.2 counts any responsibility within the previous 12 months; the rule has no minimum length of service.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, acting, temporary or rotational roles are still responsibility; test the activity and the 12 months, not how long or how officially the role was held.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Oversight around the activity that has lapsed
questions.question: Planning assurance on an Estonian freight forwarder's customs unit, internal auditor Kadri learns the unit's risk committee stopped meeting last year and nobody now reviews control exceptions. Which view of these facts is MOST accurate?

options.A: A board matter: lapsed oversight goes straight to the board
options.B: Already a finding: the lapses breach the unit's governance rules
options.C: An engagement matter: due care assesses how well these processes work
options.D: Management's matter: the unit's managers own its risk processes

questions.key_concept: Due professional care includes assessing how adequate and effective governance, risk management and control processes are, in each engagement as well as in the plan.
questions.pre_read: A dormant committee and unreviewed exceptions in processes managers own: does ownership, the board or a finding settle them, or does the engagement weigh them?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care requires internal auditors to assess how adequate and effective the governance, risk management and control processes are, and Standard 13.2 requires gathering information on those processes in the activity under review. A dormant risk committee and unreviewed exceptions therefore shape this engagement's risk assessment. The runner-up is half right: managers own these processes and fix their weaknesses, but owning them does not exempt them from the auditor's assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Governance concerns can reach the board once results are assessed and significant. At planning nothing is assessed yet, so the lapses shape what this engagement tests.
wrong_explanations.B: Kadri has only been told this. A finding needs evidence compared with criteria; for now the lapses are risk information that shapes what the engagement tests.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: managers own their processes and decide fixes, but due care still requires the internal auditor to assess how well they work. Ownership settles who acts.

tips: Eliminate: A, because nothing has been assessed yet to take to the board, and B, because a finding needs evidence measured against criteria and Kadri has only been told.
Final two: C beats D because ownership decides who fixes a weakness, while Standard 4.2 has the internal auditor assess how adequate and effective the processes are.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, management owning a process never takes it outside due care; weak oversight found at planning shapes what the engagement tests.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Two local slips with one shared cause
questions.question: Two Uruguayan dairy plants' registers each rate a cooling-log lapse low, as a local slip; planning the engagement, internal auditor Lucía traces both to the monitoring app all six plants share. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Judge the risk by the app fault's reach, with managers' input
options.B: Ask plant managers to re-rate the lapses, as owners of the registers
options.C: Weigh both lapses with each plant's managers, rating plant by plant
options.D: Recommend replacing the app now, before the risk is rated

questions.key_concept: Critical thinking connects events: a cause shared across units sets a risk's significance by its reach, and management's view is an input, not the answer.
questions.pre_read: Two small lapses, one shared app. Does the significance belong to each lapse, or to the cause, and whose judgment settles it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires internal auditors to evaluate how significant risks are, and its considerations say this takes their own knowledge, experience and critical thinking, with input from the activity's managers. Two lapses that each look local become one risk once a shared app causes both, and its reach across six plants drives significance. The runner-up hands the rating back to the register owners, whose views are one input to the auditor's own judgment.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: managers own their registers and their input counts, but the engagement's rating of significance is the internal auditor's judgment, and the shared cause is evidence for it.
wrong_explanations.C: Consulting each plant's managers is sound, but rating plant by plant treats one fault as two local events. The shared app is what makes the risk significant.
wrong_explanations.D: Recommendations come after a finding is evaluated and discussed with management, which chooses the fix. At planning, the task is to judge how significant the risk is.

tips: Eliminate: C, because consulting is sound but rating plant by plant misses the one cause behind both lapses, and D, because a fix is recommended after the finding is evaluated, and management chooses it.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 13.2's considerations make management's view an input to the internal auditor's own judgment of significance, not a substitute for it.
Exam cue: when several small events share one cause, CIA questions expect the internal auditor to judge the risk by the cause's reach, not event by event or owner by owner.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Criteria written by the seller
questions.question: Planning a first engagement on a Norwegian power utility's drone inspections of its lines, internal auditor Ingrid finds management's criteria are the drone vendor's manual. Which way of judging those criteria is BEST?

options.A: Study the manual and the vendor's training course in depth
options.B: Compare them with recommended practice and other utilities' criteria
options.C: Ask the vendor's engineers to confirm that the manual is complete
options.D: Propose advisory work, so management can write new criteria

questions.key_concept: Research tests management's criteria before relying on them: compare them with recommended practice and with other organizations' criteria.
questions.pre_read: The criteria come from the seller of the drones. Which sources can test them, and which only repeat what the seller says?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.4 Evaluation Criteria requires internal auditors to assess whether management's criteria are adequate before using them, and its considerations ask them to look up recommended practice and set management's criteria beside those other organizations use. A vendor's manual may serve the product rather than the utility's objectives, so sources independent of the vendor test it. The runner-up, the vendor's engineers, are experts, but they have a stake in their own manual.

wrong_explanations.A: Studying the manual in depth shows what it says, not whether it fits the utility's objectives. Judging adequacy needs sources beyond the document being judged.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Standard 13.4's considerations allow expert input on criteria, but the vendor's engineers have a stake in their own manual, so their confirmation adds little independent support.
wrong_explanations.D: Advisory work may follow when criteria are missing or inadequate. Here criteria exist and their adequacy is not yet known, so assessing them comes first.

tips: Eliminate: A, because studying the manual alone cannot test the manual, and D, because advisory work may follow inadequate criteria, but adequacy has not been judged yet.
Final two: B beats C because expert input helps, but the vendor's engineers judge their own product; recommended practice and peers' criteria are independent sources.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, judge criteria against sources independent of whoever wrote them; comparing with peers tests adequacy, it does not replace adequate criteria.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. A merger announced partway through the plan year
questions.question: At an Azerbaijani insurer midway through the plan year, chief audit executive Leyla learns of a merger with a rival in five months, joining both firms' claims and IT systems. What is Leyla's BEST response?

options.A: Join the merger team's briefings, and keep the current plan
options.B: Add merger work to next year's plan, for board approval
options.C: Ask senior management to decide which planned engagements to drop
options.D: Revise the current plan for the merger, for board approval

questions.key_concept: Handling change means moving the plan in time: a merger's risks start before closing, so the current plan is revised now, with board approval.
questions.pre_read: A merger five months away, with systems joined. Does the plan move now or next cycle, and is knowing about it acting?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan requires a dynamic plan, revised in time as the business, risks and systems change, with the board approving significant changes. Joining two firms' claims and IT systems in five months is such a change, and its risks start before closing, so Leyla revises the current plan now. The runner-up also seeks board approval, but adding the work to next year's plan leaves the merger's run-up uncovered.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard 11.1's considerations do have the chief audit executive kept informed of major developments, but knowing about the merger is not acting on it: the plan must change in time.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: board approval is right, but next year's plan starts after the merger closes. Standard 9.4 requires the plan to change in time, so it changes now.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management gives input on the plan; the board approves it and its significant changes. Letting senior management decide what to drop moves that approval away from the board.

tips: Eliminate: A, because staying informed without changing the plan leaves the merger's risks uncovered, and C, because senior management gives input while the board approves the plan's significant changes.
Final two: D beats B because both seek the board's approval, but Standard 9.4 keeps the plan dynamic: merger risks arise before next year's plan begins.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about change, the plan moves when the risk moves, within the current period; waiting for the next cycle is the trap.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Weighing four signs of a development need
questions.question: Compiling training requests at a Tongan bank, senior internal auditor Mele notes four situations. Which MOST clearly calls for continuing professional development now?

options.A: An auditor lacks payroll skills; payroll is not audited for two years
options.B: The chief audit executive soon approves work on an unfamiliar new law
options.C: A manager calls an auditor's upheld finding unfair in a one-off complaint
options.D: The chief audit executive wants analytics training no planned work will use

questions.key_concept: A development need is most pressing where a gap meets current or imminent responsibilities, and the chief audit executive is not exempt.
questions.pre_read: Which gap meets work that is about to start, and does the rule cover the person who approves everyone else's work?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.2 Continuing Professional Development requires every internal auditor, the chief audit executive included, to keep developing the competencies their responsibilities need, and its considerations point to learning about changes that affect the organization. Approving work soon on a law one does not know is a gap tied to imminent work. The runner-up is a real gap, but with no payroll work for two years it can wait.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a gap matters most when work needs it. With no payroll engagement for two years, this belongs in a later plan, behind a gap that meets work now.
wrong_explanations.C: Feedback signals a need when it points to how the auditor works. One complaint about a finding that review upheld is about the result, not a skill.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 3.2's considerations balance individual goals with the function's needs, so this may be funded, but training no planned work uses is a goal, not a pressing need.

tips: Eliminate: C, because one complaint about an upheld result shows no skills gap, and D, because training tied to no planned work is a goal, not a pressing need.
Final two: B beats A because Standard 3.2 binds the chief audit executive too, and B's gap meets work about to start, while A's meets no work for two years.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about development needs, look for the gap that meets current or imminent responsibilities, and exempt nobody, the chief audit executive included.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. A unit's targets that work against the strategy
questions.question: Internal auditor Jae-won's planning memo would test a Korean courier's delivery unit against on-time targets only, which it meets by air freight; the courier's strategy is cutting emissions. Which comment from supervisor Hye-jin is BEST?

options.A: Keep it: the unit is judged against the targets its managers own
options.B: Revise it to test emissions in place of the on-time targets
options.C: Revise it to weigh emissions alongside the on-time targets
options.D: Ask the chief audit executive to raise the conflict with the board

questions.key_concept: Due care weighs the organization's strategy and objectives, not only the activity's targets; a unit can meet its targets while working against the strategy.
questions.pre_read: The unit meets its own targets. Does that settle what the engagement weighs, or does the courier's strategy come in too?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care requires internal auditors to assess the organization's strategy and objectives, and Standard 13.2 requires gathering information on the strategies, objectives and risks relevant to the activity; its considerations call for examining how the activity aligns with the organization. Targets met by air freight may work against a strategy of cutting emissions, so the memo should take in that risk. The runner-up judges the unit only by its own targets.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the unit's own targets matter, but due care also weighs the organization's strategy, and a unit can meet its targets while working against it.
wrong_explanations.B: The on-time targets still matter to the courier. Due care adds the organization's strategy to the picture; it does not swap the activity's own objectives out.
wrong_explanations.D: Nothing is assessed yet. If the targets prove inadequate criteria, Standard 13.4 has auditors identify better ones through discussion with senior management or the board: planning, not escalation.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the unit's own targets still matter and are kept, and D, because escalation to the board follows assessed, accepted risk, not a planning observation.
Final two: C beats A because due care weighs the organization's strategy as well as the activity's targets, so targets met at the strategy's expense are a risk to assess.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, check that the activity's goals line up with the organization's; a target met at the strategy's expense is a risk, however successful the unit looks.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. A law that changed during the period
questions.question: Last year's engagement on a Jamaican clinic chain's records unit found no exceptions; its unchanged procedures predate a data-retention law effective in March. How should internal auditor Shanice BEST plan assurance on this calendar year?

options.A: Weigh the higher chance of noncompliance since March in testing
options.B: Repeat last year's tests, and ask managers how they apply the law
options.C: Report a legal violation now, as the procedures predate the law
options.D: Weigh it with the compliance team, and rely on its March review

questions.key_concept: Due care weighs how probable significant noncompliance is; a change in the rules during the period raises it, whatever earlier results showed.
questions.pre_read: What changed during the period under review, and can last year's clean result speak to it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care requires internal auditors to weigh how likely significant errors, fraud, noncompliance and other risks are. Procedures left unchanged since before a law took effect make noncompliance since March more likely, so testing should be aimed there and sized to it. The runner-up repeats tests set before the law existed and adds only managers' word, for which Standard 4.3 has internal auditors seek supporting evidence.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: asking managers is a fair start, but last year's tests predate the law and answers need corroboration. Due care sizes testing to the higher chance of noncompliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing has been tested yet. Outdated procedures make a breach more likely but do not prove one; testing establishes whether a violation occurred before it is reported as one.
wrong_explanations.D: Coordinating with compliance is sound, but reliance needs a documented basis, and Standard 9.5's considerations build it on an evaluation the stem does not show. Shanice still weighs the risk.

tips: Eliminate: C, because outdated procedures make a breach more likely but prove none until testing, and D, because relying on the compliance team needs an evaluation the stem does not show.
Final two: A beats B because tests set before the law cannot measure compliance with it, and managers' answers need corroboration; Standard 4.2 sizes the work to the higher probability now.

Exam cue: a change in law, system or staffing during the period raises the probability of errors or noncompliance; on CIA questions, last year's tests and managers' assurances do not cover what changed.

questions.subtopic: 1B6 Confidentiality and proper use of information. A fellow assurance provider asks for workpapers
questions.question: A Ugandan insurer's compliance team, an assurance provider internal audit coordinates with, asks engagement supervisor Okello for a claims engagement's workpapers, which hold patients' details, to avoid retesting. Which response is BEST?

options.A: Send them, since coordination calls for sharing work to avoid retesting
options.B: Send a summary of the results, and keep the workpapers back
options.C: Ask the claims manager's consent, as owner of the claims information
options.D: Route the request through the function's release steps for records

questions.key_concept: Releasing engagement records, even to a fellow assurance provider, follows the internal audit function's methodology; a good purpose does not replace the route.
questions.pre_read: The requester is inside the organization and has a sound reason. Does either fact decide whether, and what, Okello releases?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 5.2 Protection of Information bars giving confidential information to anyone not authorized and names the release of engagement records, inside or outside the organization, as a matter for the function; Standard 4.1 requires following the function's methodologies, which Standard 9.3's considerations expect to cover releases. The runner-up is right that coordination avoids retesting, but the chief audit executive runs coordination, and it does not bypass the release route.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: coordination may well end in sharing, but the chief audit executive runs it, and whether records go, and which, follows the function's release route.
wrong_explanations.B: Sharing results is a normal coordination step, but the chief audit executive runs coordination (Standard 9.5) and the release route decides what goes; a summary chosen alone skips both.
wrong_explanations.C: A claims manager's consent does not authorize release of internal audit's records; the function's route decides, applying the privacy rules that cover the patients' details.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a summary is still a release, and choosing it alone skips the route and the chief audit executive's coordination, and C, because a claims manager's consent cannot release internal audit's records.
Final two: D beats A because coordination is the chief audit executive's and explains why sharing may help, while Standards 5.2 and 4.1 leave whether and what to share to the release route.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a good purpose or a trusted requester never replaces the route for releasing engagement records; apply the methodology, then share what it allows.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. Reviews that teach auditors to stop asking
questions.question: Chief audit executive Zuzana finds that a Slovak railway's supervisors mark well-reasoned workpaper questions beyond the work program 'out of scope', and auditors have stopped asking them. Which change is BEST?

options.A: Fund a professional skepticism course for every auditor this year
options.B: Have supervisors welcome such questions, with justified changes approved
options.C: Tighten work programs so every needed step is listed in advance
options.D: Rate auditors chiefly on finishing programs within budgeted hours

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive should encourage curiosity; when reviews discourage good questions, the fix lies with the reviews, while work program changes are still approved.
questions.pre_read: The auditors already ask good questions. Where does the problem start, and which change reaches that point?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism requires an inquisitive attitude, and Standard 3.1's considerations say the chief audit executive should encourage auditors to be intellectually curious. Here the auditors already ask good questions; the supervisors' responses are teaching them to stop. Welcoming those questions, with work program changes approved as Standard 13.6 requires, removes the cause. The runner-up, skepticism training, helps auditors who lack the habit, which is not this team's problem.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 4.3's considerations have the chief audit executive build skepticism through training, but a course leaves the review practice, which stops the questions, in place.
wrong_explanations.C: Listing steps in advance makes programs complete but cannot foresee what fieldwork turns up. It would leave even less room for the questions supervisors now reject.
wrong_explanations.D: Budget adherence is a fair performance measure, but rating mainly on it rewards finishing fast and adds pressure against the questions the team has stopped asking.

tips: Eliminate: C, because no program can list in advance what fieldwork turns up, and D, because rating mainly on budgeted hours rewards stopping early, the habit to be broken.
Final two: B beats A because training builds a habit these auditors already show; the supervisors' review practice is the cause, and Standard 13.6 lets justified changes be approved.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, find where a problem starts before choosing a fix: training cures a skills gap, not a review practice that discourages questions.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Due professional care and skepticism. Risk reports the board never sees
questions.question: Drafting a Chilean salmon farmer's internal audit plan, chief audit executive Catalina reads a year of board and committee minutes: management's risk reports were not presented once. How should this BEST affect the plan?

options.A: If the reports prove unreliable, since the plan draws on them
options.B: Later: the governance audit due in two years will assess it
options.C: Now: board oversight that never sees them is a weakness to weigh
options.D: Now: raise every risk rating, since the board oversaw none of them

questions.key_concept: Due care weighs how well governance, risk management and control processes work, and the chief audit executive weighs it in the plan's risk assessment.
questions.pre_read: A board that does not see risk reports: does that weigh on the plan now or later, and as what?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2 Due Professional Care requires assessing how adequate and effective governance, risk management and control processes are, and its considerations tie that to the risk assessment behind the plan. Standard 9.1 requires the chief audit executive to understand the board's oversight of risk management, and Standard 9.4 rests the plan's assessment on that understanding. The runner-up postpones what this year's assessment needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Reliability counts when internal audit relies on management's risk information. Due care also weighs the oversight process itself, and a board that never sees the reports is weak oversight.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the governance audit will look closer, but Standard 4.2's considerations have the chief audit executive weigh these processes when assessing risk for this plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Weak oversight is itself a governance risk to weigh in the plan. It is not a reason to raise every rating; each risk is still judged on its own facts.

tips: Eliminate: A, because due care weighs the oversight process itself, not only the reports' reliability, and D, because weak oversight is a risk to weigh, not a reason to raise every rating.
Final two: C beats B because Standard 4.2's considerations put governance and risk processes into the plan's own risk assessment; a later audit adds depth, not a reason to wait.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a governance or risk management weakness found while planning shapes the plan now; a future engagement on it does not postpone the weighing.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. One queue and three possible causes
questions.question: During fieldwork at a Mongolian cashmere processor, internal auditor Bat-Erdene finds that late supplier payments all wait in one approval queue; staffing, routing rules or approval limits could explain it. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Name staffing as the cause, since the backlog points to it
options.B: Report the delays now and leave the cause for follow-up, for timeliness
options.C: Adopt the cause the payables managers give, since they know the process
options.D: Work through every possible cause with the payables managers first

questions.key_concept: Critical thinking tests every plausible cause before naming one, and Standard 14.3 has that work done with management when possible.
questions.pre_read: Three plausible causes, one queue. Is the likeliest one enough, and who helps tell them apart?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 Evaluation of Findings requires internal auditors to work with management to identify root causes when possible, and its considerations note that management may understand underlying causes better and that root cause work means asking why, step by step. Three plausible causes call for testing each with the payables managers. The runner-up settles on the likeliest cause untested; Standard 2.1 wants judgments that weigh all relevant circumstances.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a backlog may point to staffing, but naming it before testing the other two causes is a guess; Standard 14.3 has causes worked out with management.
wrong_explanations.B: Timely reporting matters, but Standard 14.3 has the root cause identified with management when possible. Here three causes can still be tested before the finding is written.
wrong_explanations.C: Managers may understand causes better, so their view is a key input, but a cause they name is still untested. The internal auditor tests each plausible cause with them.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the cause can still be found with the managers before the finding is written, and C, because a cause the managers name is an input to test, not an answer.
Final two: D beats A because a backlog can suggest staffing without proving it; Standard 14.3 has each plausible cause tested with management when possible before one is named.
Exam cue: on CIA questions with several plausible causes, the internal auditor tests each with management when possible before naming one; data alone or a manager's preference does not settle it.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Skills and competencies auditors need. A peer's mandate offered as a shortcut
questions.question: Kyrgyz bank chief audit executive Aibek has briefed the board on the Standards and banking law; before setting the mandate, a director asks Aibek for a peer bank's mandate to copy. Which reply is BEST?

options.A: Offer research on leading audit functions, fitted to this bank
options.B: Offer a peer-bank survey, and the mandate most of them use
options.C: Offer the peer bank's mandate, adjusted to this bank's size and risks
options.D: Decline, as setting the mandate is the board's task, not Aibek's

questions.key_concept: Research uses many sources: the chief audit executive informs the mandate with research on leading audit functions, fitted to the organization, not one peer's model.
questions.pre_read: A director wants one peer's mandate. How many sources should inform the board's decision, and whose job is it to supply them?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.1 Internal Audit Mandate requires the chief audit executive to give the board and senior management the information they need to set the mandate, and its considerations list research on how leading internal audit functions work beside the Standards and the law. Standard 6.2's considerations accept charter models but have them customized. The runner-up customizes one peer's model: one source, not research.

wrong_explanations.B: A survey widens the sources, but the most common mandate is not necessarily a leading one, and taking it as it stands ignores this bank's own needs.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: adapting a model can help, but one peer's mandate is one source. The considerations of Standard 6.1 point to research into leading functions before the board decides.
wrong_explanations.D: The board sets the mandate, but Standard 6.1 requires the chief audit executive to give it the information needed to do so. Declining leaves the director's question unanswered.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the most common mandate is not necessarily a leading one or a fit for this bank, and D, because the chief audit executive must supply the information the board needs.
Final two: A beats C because Standard 6.1's considerations point to research into leading internal audit functions; one peer's mandate, however well adjusted, is a single source.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about research, look for several sources weighed for fit, not one convenient model, however well it is adjusted.
